name: Dark Blue Grey
lede: Dark Blue Grey is a deep, muted blue-grey from the 2010 xkcd color survey, built by adding *dark* to the already-compound name Blue Grey, and it reads as more blue than most greys of its depth.

sections.title: Dark plus an existing compound
sections.body: The name is built in two steps: the xkcd survey already records a plain [[blue-grey]], and volunteers separately typed a darker version of it, which the library files as its own entry [1][2]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS system catalogues the same hue as dark grayish blue, four units away in CIEDE2000, close enough to call the same family [2]. In Munsell notation it falls at 9.7B 2.3/3.3, a dark, weakly chromatic blue [2]. Measured in LCH it has lightness 24, chroma 15 and hue 252 degrees, nearer to [[slate]] and [[navy]] than to [[charcoal]], though all three sit within a few units of it [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our 23,781-painting archive, a color within six units of Dark Blue Grey covers at least one per cent of the canvas in 264 paintings, about 1.1 percent of the archive, as photographed; the stricter within-painting lens, which asks whether it is one of a painting's dominant colors, finds it in 127 [3]. That makes it more common than 63 percent of the named colors the archive tracks [3]. It most often plays a hidden color, sitting in a painting's darker, less noticed areas in 55 percent of the 127 [3].

Its earliest match in the archive, Master of the Franciscan Crucifixes' panel dated 1270, is 740 years before the name itself is recorded, in the 2010 survey; that gap is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof that the pigment or dye existed under this name, or at all, that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. Paul Gauguin is its most devoted painter here, carrying it in 6 of his 50 archived works, about 6.6 times the rate of the museums those paintings come from [3]. In printed English the phrase peaked in the 1940s [4].
